 Fewer South Dakotans receiving SNAP benefits, new study finds 
 Download the KOTA News App. By Tamara Chibe Published : Nov. 12, 2026 at 8:00 PM CST | Updated : 4 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google RAPID CITY, S.D. (KOTA) - Fewer South Dakotans are relying on federal food assistance than they were a year ago, but the average amount recipients receive has increased slightly, according to a new study.
 An analysis from financial technology company SmartAsset found the number of South Dakota residents receiving Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits dropped 6.8% between 2025 and 2026.
 SNAP, formerly known as food stamps, helps eligible low-income individuals and families pay for groceries.
 Researchers estimate about 8% of South Dakota’s population currently receives benefits. Despite the decline in participation, the average amount paid to recipients in the state increased 1.5% over the past year.
 South Dakota’s decline is part of a broader national trend. SNAP participation fell in 49 states, with Alaska being the only state to report an increase.
 Nationwide, about 36 million Americans received SNAP benefits in mid-2026, down from nearly 42 million in 2025.
 The study points to changes under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act as one factor behind the decline. The legislation expanded federal work requirements for certain SNAP recipients and shifted more of the program’s costs to states.
 Under the changes, work requirements were expanded to include adults ages 55 to 64 and some parents with children ages 14 and older. The law also removed certain exemptions previously available to veterans, people experiencing homelessness and former foster youth under age 25.
 Participation rates vary widely across the country.
 New Mexico had the highest share of residents receiving SNAP benefits, with more than 20% of its population enrolled. Utah and neighboring Wyoming had the lowest rates, with just over 4% of residents receiving assistance.
 Although enrollment declined in most states, average monthly benefits increased in 22 states. Researchers said benefit amounts can change based on cost-of-living adjustments, household income and family size.
 SmartAsset’s analysis used the latest available federal SNAP data through May 2026 to compare participation rates and benefit amounts across all 50 states.
